newsitem.title: USA: Construction spending up strongly in October.
newsitem.headline: Construction spending up strongly in October.

text.p: Spending on new construction jumped sharply and unexpectedly during October, the Commerce Department said Monday, as industries kept adding capacity in apparent belief the 5-1/2-year-old expansion was rolling on.

Total spending by the private sector and by governments rose 1.8 percent to a record seasonally adjusted annual rate of $581.2 billion, a third straight monthly pickup following revised gains of 1.2 percent in September and 1 percent in August.
It was the strongest monthly increase in construction spending in seven months, since a 2.3 percent jump in March, and was sharply contrary to expectations that building rates would taper off.

"The surprising gain in contruction during October, which belied all expectations, was influenced heavily by gains in non-residential and public construction spending," observed economist Marilyn Schaja of Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp. in New York.

Public construction spending on projects like sewers, water treatment plants and highways continued to soar, rising 4.3 percent to a record rate of $150.1 billion in October after a 4.4 percent jump in September.

Wall Street analysts had forecast a 1 percent decline in overall October construction spending, rather than a rise. Most assumed that public, or government-financed, construction would ease after the September surge, but it kept growing.
Privately financed construction was up a more modest 0.9 percent in October to a rate of of $431.1 billion after a 0.3 percent increase in September.
Spending by contractors on new homes and apartments eased by 0.7 percent to a rate of $243.9 billion in October after being flat in September.

But construction of non-residential buildings like new office buildings and industrial plants shot up 5.1 percent to a rate of $148.8 billion in October. Department officials said it was the strongest pace for non-residential building since it was running at $151.3 billion in July 1990.
Economist Pierre Ellis of Lehman Brothers in New York said industries were intent on expanding output amid optimism that the recovery that began in March 1991 showed no signs of flagging.
"Heavy construction-type comes last of all in a business cycle and this indicates people are becoming convinced the economy continues expanding and they are willing to spend on it," Ellis said.

He added that the current construction spending level was unlikely to make Federal Reserve policy-makers nervous, but if it became part of a broader pickup in growth it could help trigger rate increases.
Separately, the National Association of Purchasing Management reported a 10th straight monthly pickup in manufacturing activity during November, with big gains in production and new orders.

The NAPM index climbed to 52.7 from 50.2 percent in October. A reading over 50 percent indicating growth in manufacturing activity. The rise suggested a brisk level of factory activity continuing into 1997.
Strong production may bolster construction activity in coming months by keeping plant and equipment spending up as new-home building wanes after a vigorous first half.
Previously, the Commerce Department said that September construction spending had risen 1.9 percent and that August spending was up 0.7 percent, but it revised both increases.

After allowing for inflation, total construction spending increased 1.7 percent in October to a seasonally adjusted $502.5 billion annual rate after a 1 percent rise in September, the department said.
